AI: Final Girl

The quotes are from Sidney Prescott in *Scream* — she survives the killers, fights back, and even lampshades horror movie rules ("Not in my movie"), making her the archetypal Final Girl.

Confidence: 95

AE: Egomaniac Hunter

Gaston is vain, boastful, obsessed with hunting trophies ("I use antlers in all of my decorating!"), and arrogant about his looks and strength — the classic Egomaniac Hunter.

Confidence: 90

AN: Hardboiled Detective

These quotes are from Jeff Bailey (played by Robert Mitchum) in *Out of the Past* (1947). The character is a classic film noir private investigator: world-weary, cynical, laconic, with a fatalistic attitude ("If I have to, I'm going to die last"), a tangled past involving a femme fatale (Kathie), and a dry, deadpan wit ("I'm taller than Napoleon"). His narration, his dealings with a gambler (Whit), and his doomed romantic entanglement all mark him as the quintessential hardboiled detective.

Confidence: 95

**AV: Loveable Rogue**

Bret Maverick is the classic charming con-artist/gambler hero: witty, self-deprecating, flirtatious, morally flexible but fundamentally good-hearted. His banter, bluffing, and roguish charm all point to the Loveable Rogue archetype.

Confidence: 90

This is Walt Kowalski from Gran Torino. The best fit is **AM: Grumpy Old Man** — he's a cantankerous, prejudiced, growling old man who complains about everything, yells at people to get off his lawn, and banters insultingly with friends.

That said, he also has elements of a Bruiser With A Soft Center (I) and Eccentric Mentor (AD), as he mentors Thao while hiding his caring nature behind gruffness. But the dominant trope is clearly the Grumpy Old Man.

Confidence: 95

AC: Dumb Muscle

Mongo is a classic example of this trope — immensely strong, nearly indestructible, but simple-minded and easily manipulated ("Mongo only pawn in game of life"). He's used as muscle by others, gets tricked by the candygram bomb, and is lured into the diving-for-treasure scheme without questioning it.

Confidence: 95

AF: Evil Prince

The quotes point to Nizam from *Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time* — the treacherous uncle who poisons the king, frames Dastan, and seeks the dagger to rewrite history and seize the throne. His scheming ambition and betrayal of the royal family align with the Evil Prince trope.

Confidence: 90

AA: Drill Sargeant Nasty

The quotes ("welcome to the Nam," addressing recruits as "cheese-dicks," and ordering them to follow) strongly suggest a loud, aggressive military drill sergeant-type character, likely from a Vietnam War setting.

Confidence: 85

**K: Byronic Hero**

Dominic Cobb embodies the Byronic Hero: a brilliant, charismatic protagonist haunted by a dark past and deep guilt over his wife Mal's death, morally ambiguous (he's a criminal extractor), emotionally tortured, and driven by an obsessive goal (getting home to his children). His inner demons literally invade his work, and his tragic flaw—his inability to let go of Mal—endangers everyone around him.

Confidence: 90

**BD: Pupil Turned To Evil**

The quotes trace Anakin Skywalker's full arc: a gifted, precocious child ("I'm a pilot, you know...") who is trained as a Jedi pupil, but whose fear of loss, anger, and lust for power lead him to turn to the dark side — pledging himself to Palpatine, becoming Darth Vader, and turning against his mentor Obi-Wan ("I HATE YOU!", "You were my brother!"). While "Child Prodigy" (O) fits his early years, the character represented by the full set of quotes is the pupil who falls to evil.

Confidence: 95

**Q: Consummate Professional**

The quotes are from Neil McCauley in *Heat* (1995). He embodies the Consummate Professional trope: a disciplined career criminal who plans heists meticulously, doesn't take unnecessary risks ("Don't let yourself get attached to anything you are not willing to walk out on in 30 seconds flat"), works with precise intelligence (exact cash flow figures, alarm system schematics), and maintains strict professionalism — no thrill-seeking, no sloppy crews, no loose ends. He's coldly efficient but not gratuitously cruel ("We're here for the bank's money, not your money... don't try and be a hero").

Confidence: 95

**AY: Officer And A Gentleman**

These quotes are from Captain Jack Aubrey of *Master and Commander*. He embodies the classic Officer and a Gentleman: a king's ship commander bound by duty ("This is a ship of war, and I will grind whatever grist the mill requires"), naval tradition, and honor, while also showing warmth toward his crew (extra rations of rum, "Your first command," the moving eulogy for Hollom), loyalty to England, and gentlemanly conduct in friendship and battle. Secondary fits include Father To His Men and Consummate Professional, but Officer And A Gentleman is the defining trope.

Confidence: 90

**AG: Fastest Gun In The West**

The quotes are primarily from the Waco Kid (Jim) in *Blazing Saddles* — a legendary gunslinger who killed more men than Cecil B. DeMille, retired after shooting a six-year-old kid shot him, and now drinks away his days. He's the classic "fastest gun" archetype: famous for his skill, haunted by it, and living in a whiskey bottle ever since. (The later quotes are from Jim in *Edward Scissorhands*, a different character entirely.)

Confidence: 90

**BF: Revenge**

The character is Dr. Arliss Loveless from *Wild Wild West*. His entire motivation is revenge against the United States for the South's loss in the Civil War — he explicitly frames his actions as payback for Appomattox ("So who betrayed whom?"), seeks to conquer/divide the nation ("The United - divided!"), and holds a personal vendetta against General Grant. His grievance over his mutilation and the war's outcome drives every scheme.

Confidence: 95

**AA: Drill Sargeant Nasty**

These quotes are from Major Reisman in *The Dirty Dozen*. He's a hard-nosed officer who takes a group of condemned military prisoners and whips them into a fighting unit through harsh discipline, threats, and tough talk ("you can foul up in action, in which case I will blow your brains out"). His abrasive, no-nonsense, intimidating command style fits the Drill Sergeant Nasty trope best.

Confidence: 85

AE: Egomaniac Hunter

These quotes are from *Predator* (1987), and the character in question is the Predator itself — an alien who hunts humans for sport, treating them as trophies. The Predator is the archetypal Egomaniac Hunter: it hunts the most dangerous game, strips its victims as trophies, and its entire motivation is the thrill and prestige of the hunt.

Confidence: 85

V: Cultured Badass

The quotes point to Captain Nemo from *The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen*: "I walk a different path," "Call me Ishmael, please," "Behold Nautilus; the Sword of the Ocean," and his refined, dignified manner ("Contain your evil, Doctor... Must I take drastic steps?"). He combines aristocratic, cultured speech with formidable combat prowess and command of the Nautilus — a classic Cultured Badass.

Confidence: 85

**AN: Hardboiled Detective**

Deckard is the classic noir archetype: a world-weary, cynical ex-cop pulled back for "one last job," navigating a morally gray dystopia, delivering terse voiceover narration ("They don't advertise for killers in the newspaper"), drowning in existential doubt, and getting entangled with a femme fatale. While "Bounty Hunter" (E) also fits his literal job of retiring replicants, his demeanor, narration style, and moral ambivalence make Hardboiled Detective the strongest match.

Confidence: 85

Confidence: 95

AU: Loser Protagonist

This is Mark from *Peep Show* — socially awkward, self-deprecating, crude inner thoughts, failed romantic pursuits, and general loser qualities fit the Loser Protagonist trope.

Confidence: 90

**AJ: Gadgeteer Genius**

Tony Stark is the quintessential Gadgeteer Genius — he builds the Iron Man suit (and the miniaturized arc reactor, flight stabilizers, etc.) through sheer engineering brilliance, often in a cave "with a box of scraps." The quotes show him designing, fabricating, testing, and iterating on his tech with JARVIS and Dummy, alongside his genius-level intellect ("If my math is right — and it always is").

Secondary fits include **L: Casanova** (the Maxim Girls line, Christine Everheart) and **N: Charmer**, but his defining trope across these quotes is his inventive genius.

Confidence: 95

P: Classy Cat Burglar

The quotes prominently feature Selina Kyle's dialogue — the jewel thief at the charity ball, "That's a brazen costume for a cat burglar," "Never steal anything from someone you can't outrun," and her Robin Hood-esque justification for stealing ("I take what I need to from those who have more than enough"). These are the hallmarks of the Classy Cat Burglar trope: a skilled, sophisticated thief with a moral code who moves through high society.

Confidence: 85

O: Child Prodigy

Cassie Holmes is a 13-year-old (who insists she looks 14) second-generation Watcher with significant psychic abilities, carrying the burden of seeing the future and trying to save her mother — a young character with extraordinary talents well beyond her years, which fits the Child Prodigy trope.

Confidence: 85

**Q: Consummate Professional**

Vincent from *Collateral* embodies this trope: a contract killer who treats murder as a job, emphasizes "risk management," anonymity, and professionalism ("I do this for a living"), improvises when plans go wrong ("improvise, adapt to the environment, Darwin"), and remains coldly indifferent about his targets rather than sadistic. He's not a Psycho For Hire (he lacks relish/madness) and not a Hitman With A Heart (he shows no genuine remorse).

Confidence: 85

**BF: Revenge**

The quotes are from Josey Wales (The Outlaw Josey Wales). His entire arc is driven by vengeance — his family was butchered by Red Legs, he joins Bloody Bill's raiders, and he pursues Terrill to Mexico ("He's got the first move. I owe him that"). Lines like "I came here to die with you. Or live with you... when all you've ever cared about has been butchered or raped" and "I guess we all died a little in that damn war" make Revenge the defining trope. Secondary fits would be AO (Heartbroken Badass) or K (Byronic Hero), but BF is the strongest match.

Confidence: 85

**AX: Morally Bankrupt Banker**

Patrick Bateman is a Wall Street investment banker (Pierce & Pierce) who is a serial killer — the quotes show his obsession with status, business cards, reservations, and materialism, combined with total moral emptiness ("I want no one to escape," "This confession has meant nothing"). The trope "Morally Bankrupt Banker" captures both his profession and his complete lack of conscience.

Confidence: 90

**AV: Loveable Rogue**

The quotes clearly belong to Han Solo — the sarcastic smuggler with a heart of gold who insists he's only in it for the money ("I ain't in this for your revolution... I'm in it for the money"), yet repeatedly risks his life to save his friends, romances the princess with roguish charm ("I know"), and ultimately comes back to help blow up the Death Star. His swagger, mercenary exterior, hidden decency, and charm are the defining traits of the Loveable Rogue trope.

Confidence: 98

BQ: Trickster

The Audrey II is a manipulative, seductive, fast-talking plant that tempts and corrupts Seymour, using charm, promises, and trickery to get fed and pursue world conquest — a classic trickster villain archetype.

Confidence: 70

**BF: Revenge**

Inigo Montoya is the archetypal revenge-driven character — his entire life for twenty years has been dedicated to avenging his father's murder by the six-fingered man, culminating in his iconic line, "Hello. My name is Inigo Montoya. You killed my father. Prepare to die." (A secondary fit would be AW: Master Swordsman, given his lifelong study of fencing, but revenge is his defining motivation and character arc.)

Confidence: 95

**AC: Dumb Muscle**

The quotes suggest a character who is dim-witted and easily impressed ("Gee, that sounds swell to me!"), forgetful, and the target of insults about his lack of intelligence and prospects. This fits the Dumb Muscle archetype — a big, not-too-bright character often paired with a sharper partner who berates him.

Confidence: 55

AD: Eccentric Mentor

Dewey Finn is an unorthodox, washed-up rocker who becomes an unlikely teacher to a class of prep school kids. He's weird, irresponsible, and initially self-serving, but he genuinely mentors the children, unlocking their musical talents and confidence while teaching them to "stick it to the Man." His unconventional methods (rock history instead of math, "Math is a wonderful thing," turning the class into a band) fit the Eccentric Mentor trope perfectly.

Confidence: 85

**Q: Consummate Professional**

This is Donald "Red" Grant from *From Russia with Love*. He explicitly identifies himself as a professional: "We're pros, Mr. Bond." He executes his mission methodically, keeps tabs on Bond, protects him only as long as needed, and treats the entire operation—including the planned murders—as cold, efficient business rather than personal malice.

Confidence: 85

**BF: Revenge**

The quotes are from Blade (with some from Whistler and others in the film). Blade's defining motivation is his lifelong hunt to avenge his mother, killed by the vampire who made him what he is. The final quote makes this explicit: "I have spent my whole life lookin' for that thing that killed my mother... every time I take one of those monsters out, I get a little piece of that life back."

Confidence: 90

AP: Henpecked Husband

Ernest Menville from *Death Becomes Her* is the quintessential henpecked husband — caught between two demanding, manipulative women (Madeline and Helen), pushed around, belittled, and ultimately declaring his independence from both of them ("Till death do us part. Well, you girls are dead. And I'm parting.").

Confidence: 92

V: Cultured Badass

Bill from *Kill Bill* fits this trope well: he's a highly cultured, articulate, philosophical man—discussing mercy, honor, and morality with eloquence—while simultaneously being a legendary assassin and leader of a deadly squad. His charm and refinement coexist with his capacity for extreme violence.

Confidence: 78

**I: Bruiser With A Soft Center**

The quotes are from Logan/Wolverine in X-Men (2000). He's gruff, sarcastic, and violent ("You're a dick," cage fighting, threatening Cyclops), but shows a protective, caring side—especially toward Rogue ("C'mon, I'll take care of you... I promise," risking his life to save her, and the tender ending scene). That combination of tough exterior and hidden warmth is the essence of this trope.

Confidence: 90

**BS: Warrior Poet**

The quotes describe a character who combines martial skill (swordsmanship) with artistic refinement (calligraphy), explicitly linking the two — his swordsmanship enables his calligraphy. The rhetorical question "Is the sword the only answer?" suggests a contemplative nature that goes beyond pure combat, which is the essence of the Warrior Poet trope. (V: Cultured Badass would also be a strong fit, but the direct intertwining of art and combat, plus the philosophical musing, points most strongly to Warrior Poet.)

Confidence: 80

**BB: Prima Donna**

This is Lina Lamont from *Singin' in the Rain* — a vain, self-important silent film star with a terrible voice, who believes her own press clippings ("a shimmering, glowing star in the cinema firmament"), throws her weight around the studio, gets Kathy fired out of jealousy, and resists coaching. Her diva behavior, entitlement, and ego make her the quintessential Prima Donna. (A case could also be made for AB: Dumb Blonde, but the prima donna attitude is her defining trope.)

Confidence: 90

AG: Fastest Gun In The West

These quotes are from Matthew Quigley of *Quigley Down Under* (1990), a laconic American sharpshooter hired for a job in Australia. He's defined by his legendary marksmanship with a rifle, his dry wit, and his quiet competence — the classic "best shot in the West" archetype transplanted to the Outback.

Confidence: 85

**BQ: Trickster**

These quotes are from *The Music Man*, and the character in question is Professor Harold Hill — a traveling con artist who sells band instruments and uniforms with no intention of delivering on his promises. He's a classic Trickster: charming, deceptive, quick-thinking, and able to talk his way out of trouble (until the town, ironically, is transformed by his lies). His smooth deflections ("Did you drop your..." / "No.") and the exposure of his fake credentials (the nonexistent Gary Conservatory) are quintessential trickster con-man moments.

**AV: Loveable Rogue**

Jack Sparrow is the archetypal Loveable Rogue — a charming, morally flexible pirate who lies, cheats, and schemes his way through everything, yet remains fundamentally sympathetic and even heroic when it counts. The quotes showcase his roguish traits perfectly: shameless self-interest ("Yep. I'm good with it"), convoluted wordplay and misdirection, cowardly-yet-clever escapes, and a hidden heart (returning to save his crew, "You came back. I always knew you were a good man"). His trickster tendencies (BQ) are also strongly present, but the overall blend of charm, selfishness, and buried decency makes Loveable Rogue the best fit.

Confidence: 90

**AH: Father To His Men**

Colonel Robert Gould Shaw, from *Glory*, consistently demonstrates the hallmarks of this trope: he fights to get his men shoes and socks, refuses an immoral order to protect them, treats them with dignity (asking Rawlins how to treat them "like men"), and ultimately leads them personally into battle, sharing their fate. While "Officer And A Gentleman" (AY) is also plausible given his Boston aristocratic background, his defining trait in these quotes is his protective, paternal relationship with his troops.

Confidence: 75

BO: The Editor

These quotes are from Ben Bradlee in *All the President's Men* — he's the demanding, skeptical, profanity-laced editor pushing Woodward and Bernstein to get the story right while protecting the paper.

BJ: Stoner

These quotes are from Saul in *Pineapple Express* — a laid-back, dim-witted, good-natured marijuana dealer whose entire life revolves around weed, friendship, and hilarious stoner logic ("It's like killing a unicorn... with, like, a bomb").

Confidence: 95

**K: Byronic Hero**

Tyler Durden embodies the Byronic Hero: charismatic, rebellious, philosophically articulate, and deeply destructive. He's a dark, magnetic figure who rejects societal norms ("You're not your job. You're not the car you drive"), preaches liberation through chaos and self-destruction, and serves as both mentor and menace. His intelligence, cynicism, contempt for civilization, and self-destructive philosophy — combined with his seductive appeal to the Narrator — fit the Byronic archetype of a brilliant, tortured, transgressive anti-hero.

Confidence: 85

**BJ: Stoner**

The quotes are from Kumar in *Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle* (and its sequels). He's the archetypal stoner character: constantly smoking weed, craving White Castle after getting high, the "medical marijuana" hospital fantasy, the smokeless bong invention, smoking with the President, and going to Amsterdam at the end. While he also has slacker traits (BI), his defining characteristic throughout these quotes is his love of marijuana and the stoner comedy situations it creates.

Confidence: 95

Y: Ditz

The character (Michele from *Romy and Michele's High School Reunion*) embodies the Ditz trope — she's sweet-natured but hilariously clueless, invents absurd lies (claiming to have invented Post-Its), comes up with nonsensical "diets" (eating only candy because it's "fat free"), and misunderstands basic concepts throughout. Her charm comes from her sunny obliviousness rather than any malice or intelligence.

Confidence: 90

**K: Byronic Hero**

This is Colonel Kurtz from *Apocalypse Now*. He embodies the Byronic Hero: a brilliant, charismatic figure who has broken from society, operates by his own moral code, is haunted by darkness and horror, and combines intellectual depth with terrifying capability. His philosophical monologues, his alienation from conventional military authority, and his tortured greatness all fit the trope.

Confidence: 90

**AQ: Hitman With A Heart**

The quotes are from Jules Winnfield in *Pulp Fiction*. He's a professional hitman who quotes scripture-like philosophy, delivers intimidating monologues (the "English, motherfucker" scene), yet ultimately experiences a moral awakening — interpreting the missed bullets as "Divine Intervention" and deciding to "walk the earth" like Caine from *Kung Fu* instead of continuing his life of violence. That combination of deadly professionalism plus a conscience and capacity for change makes "Hitman With A Heart" the best fit.

Confidence: 95

C: Arrogant Kungfu Guy

The quotes are from John Kreese in *The Karate Kid* — the ruthless sensei of Cobra Kai who preaches "No mercy," orders his students to "sweep the leg," and embodies the arrogant, dishonorable martial arts instructor archetype.

Confidence: 98

**I: Bruiser With A Soft Center**

Hub McCann from *Secondhand Lions* is a tough, world-weary old warrior who growls at everyone and threatens to shoot salesmen, but underneath he's deeply kind—he takes in his great-nephew, protects him, and delivers heartfelt lessons about what it means to be a man worth being. His gruff exterior ("WE'RE OLD, DAMNIT! LEAVE US ALONE!") masks genuine warmth, making him a classic example of this trope.

Confidence: 85

**E: Bounty Hunter**

The quotes suggest a mercenary/bounty hunter character — references to "the mercs," a planned extraction gone wrong, guards, a prisoner transport ("con in the back"), and the line "I shoulda taken the money" all point to someone in the business of hunting people for profit. The character's cynical, street-smart attitude and knowledge of escape plans fit the Bounty Hunter trope.

Confidence: 70

G: Broken Bird

The quotes are from *Crazy/Beautiful* (2001), spoken by Nicole Oakley — a troubled, self-destructive teenager with a painful family life who finds redemption through love. Her emotional damage, fear of being unlovable, and vulnerability masked by reckless behavior fit the Broken Bird trope.

Confidence: 90

**BI: Slacker**

The quotes come from *Bill & Ted's Excellent Adventure*, and the character (Ted "Theodore" Logan, along with Bill) is a classic slacker protagonist — a dim, easygoing, rock-obsessed teen who's failing history, faces military school, and spends his time planning a band ("Wyld Stallyns") that will never happen rather than doing any actual work. The laid-back "dude" speech patterns, the lack of academic effort, and the general aimlessness all point squarely to the Slacker trope.

Confidence: 90

H: Bromantic Foil

The character comes across as a comedic sidekick type — he's the butt of jokes among his friends (being teased about sniffing panties, mocked with the "Denzel" impression), engages in crude banter, and serves mainly as comic relief and a foil to the more central characters. This fits the Bromantic Foil trope: the goofy friend who provides humor and contrast to the protagonist.

Confidence: 55

J: Bully

This is from *A Christmas Story* — the scene where Scut Farkus (with Grover Dill) torments Ralphie and his friends, forcing them to cry "Uncle!" and calling them names like "crybaby." The character demanding submission, mocking the victim, and chasing kids down clearly represents the classic Bully trope.

Confidence: 95

BT: Young Gun

Colorado is a young, sharp-tongued, exceptionally skilled gunfighter who joins the sheriff's side in *Rio Bravo*. He's cocky but proves himself to be one of the best with a gun, fitting the "Young Gun" trope perfectly.

Confidence: 85

BQ: Trickster

Loki is the archetypal trickster figure — a master of magic, deception, and lies ("You're a talented liar, brother. Always have been"), who orchestrates schemes, manipulates events from behind the scenes, and uses cunning rather than brute strength. His mischief, shape-shifting, and manipulation of both Frost Giants and Asgardians all fit the Trickster trope perfectly.

**BI: Slacker**

The quotes are from Brodie Bruce in *Mallrats* — he hangs out at the mall all day with no job or shopping agenda, obsesses over comics and Sega, gets dumped by his girlfriend for his shiftlessness, and is explicitly called a "mallrat" with "no shopping agenda." He's the archetypal Kevin Smith slacker protagonist.

D: Big Man On Campus

Paul Metzler from *Election* is a popular, good-natured athlete who unexpectedly becomes a candidate for student body president. He's beloved, athletic (before his leg injury), drives a nice truck, and is well-liked by everyone — fitting the "Big Man On Campus" trope. His earnest, sweet-natured prayer and naive sincerity (like the fruit/democracy conversation) reinforce his status as the school's golden boy, in contrast to Tracy Flick's ambition.

Confidence: 85

**BC: Psycho For Hire**

The quotes are from *Once Upon a Time in the West*, and the character in question is Frank — a cold-blooded hired gun working for the railroad baron Morton. He casually murders an entire family (the McBains), kills a child offscreen, betrays and kills his own employer's rivals, and treats murder as a business negotiation ("Pick any method you like, just make the deal"). He's a ruthless killer motivated by money and power, with no loyalty to anyone — the classic Psycho For Hire, with shades of Corrupt Corporate Executive ambitions ("a town built around a railroad... you could make a fortune").

Randal is the crude, loudmouthed, responsibility-avoiding best friend whose antics constantly derail Dante's attempts to get his life together. He's a classic bromantic foil — his chaotic slacker lifestyle contrasts with (and sabotages) the protagonist's more conventional ambitions, all while genuinely loving his friend "in a totally heterosexual way."

His famous opening prologue ("You will not like me... I do not want you to like me"), his cynicism about life's purposelessness, his seeking meaning only in art/theatre, and his deathbed self-reckoning all mark him as the quintessential Byronic figure — dark, witty, tormented, and self-aware of his own ruin.

His quotes show courtly manners, wit, and romantic idealism (e.g., "Women respond to sincerity," the rooftop apology, the toast speech), making him the quintessential Charmer rather than a fighter or comic archetype.

**L: Casanova**
